beats.note: The game that made it famous started as a homework deadline, not a design plan.

beats.name: Rawitsch, Heinemann and Dillenberger
beats.role: Three student teachers at a Minneapolis junior high, building from a butcher-paper map game Rawitsch had used to teach a history unit.

beats.text: Coded at a teleprinter next to the janitor's closet.
beats.note: Working on a shared HP 2100 minicomputer, they wrote roughly 800 lines of BASIC, finishing just in time for Rawitsch's class to play it on 3 December 1971.

beats.text: The original code didn't survive the semester.
beats.note: District policy wiped the mainframe afterward. Rawitsch rebuilt the game from memory three years later after joining Minnesota's educational computing agency — and that rewrite is the version that spread to schools everywhere.

beats.text: Paul Dillenberger's own summary of what the game earned him: 'a jean jacket and a copy of the game, instead of owning an island somewhere.'

beats.line: A two-week homework project became one of the best-known games ever made.
